parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: constant speed with changing velocity direction
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the word uniform tells you about how fast the object moves, and what circular tells you about the direction it moves in.
Hint 2: Remember that both velocity and acceleration are vectors, so consider how their size and their direction each behave, and how they point relative to each other.
parts.proper_answer: Speed is constant so velocity and acceleration both have constant magnitude. Velocity is tangential and acceleration is radially inward, so velocity is always perpendicular to acceleration.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort out speed versus velocity**
Uniform means the speed stays the same. But velocity is a vector, so even at constant speed the direction keeps changing as the object goes round the circle. That means the velocity vector is always tangent to the circle and constantly turning.

Step 2: **Describe the acceleration**
Because velocity is changing in direction, there must be an acceleration. In uniform motion its size stays constant and it always points toward the centre of the circle. That is the centripetal acceleration.

Step 3: **Put the two together**
A tangent line is always at $90^{\circ}$ to a radius. So: $$ \text{velocity perpendicular to acceleration at all times} $$ Both vectors keep constant magnitude but continuously change direction.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how far the ball travels in one full revolution compared with the angle it sweeps through, and how dividing each by time gives linear speed and angular speed.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link linear and angular motion**
In time $T$ for one revolution, distance travelled is circumference $2\pi R$ and angle swept is $2\pi$ rad. So linear speed is $v = 2\pi R / T$ and angular speed is $\omega = 2\pi / T$.

Step 2: **Combine to eliminate T**
Comparing the two gives: $$ v = R\omega $$ Larger radius or faster turning both give larger linear speed.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Start from a familiar form for centripetal acceleration that uses radius and one type of speed, either linear or angular.
Hint 2: Use your result from (b)(i) to replace the radius $R$ so that only $v$ and $\omega$ remain.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall a standard centripetal form**
For uniform circular motion the inward acceleration can be written as: $$ a = R\omega^2 $$ or equivalently $$ a = \frac{v^2}{R} $$

Step 2: **Eliminate R using v = R omega**
From (b)(i), $R = v/\omega$. Substitute into $a = R\omega^2$: $$ a = \left(\frac{v}{\omega}\right)\omega^2 = v\omega $$ This is the centripetal acceleration directed toward O.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at triangle OBP in Fig. 1.1 and identify which side is the hypotenuse and which side is the displacement $x$ opposite the angle $\theta$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the right-angled triangle**
OP is perpendicular to the screen and the light rays project the ball position straight onto the screen. So triangle with vertices O, B and the foot below P is right-angled, with hypotenuse OB $= R$ and opposite side $= x$.

Step 2: **Apply sine**
By definition $\sin\theta = \text{opposite}/\text{hypotenuse} = x/R$. Hence: $$ x = R\sin\theta $$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about the definition of angular speed as rate of change of angle when starting from zero angle at $t = 0$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use constant angular speed**
Angular speed is $\omega = \Delta\theta / \Delta t$. With $\theta = 0$ at $t = 0$ and $\omega$ constant: $$ \theta = \omega t $$ The angle grows steadily with time.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Consider how to combine your geometric result linking $x$ to $\theta$ with your time result linking $\theta$ to $t$.
parts.proper_answer: Substituting $\theta = \omega t$ into $x = R\sin\theta$ gives $x = R\sin\omega t$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Substitute angle versus time into displacement versus angle**
You have $x = R\sin\theta$ and $\theta = \omega t$. Replacing $\theta$: $$ x = R\sin(\omega t) $$ That is the required projection equation.

parts.label: (c)(iv)
hints: Hint 1: Recall the standard mathematical shape of displacement against time for simple harmonic motion about equilibrium at P.
parts.proper_answer: Equation is of form $x = x_0\sin\omega t$ with constant amplitude $R$, which is the defining displacement-time relation for SHM.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise the SHM form**
Simple harmonic motion has displacement varying sinusoidally with time: $$ x = x_0 \sin\omega t $$ Here $x = R\sin\omega t$ matches exactly with amplitude $x_0 = R$. So the shadow oscillates sinusoidally about P and can be modelled as SHM.

parts.label: (d)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how far the shadow can move from the centre P when the ball is at the extreme side of its circle, compared with the given diameter.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Amplitude is the radius**
From (c), maximum $|x| = R$. Diameter $= 0.46\text{ m}$, so: $$ R = \frac{0.46}{2} = 0.23\text{ m} $$ Hence amplitude of shadow $= 0.23\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Remember the link between the time for one full oscillation and the rate at which phase angle advances.
Hint 2: Rearrange that link to make the period the subject and insert $\omega = 1.9\text{ rad s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Relate omega to period**
One full cycle is $2\pi$ rad in time $T$: $$ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} $$

Step 2: **Calculate T**
Rearranging: $$ T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{1.9} = 3.3\text{ s} $$ The shadow takes the same time as one circle of the ball.

parts.label: (d)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall how peak acceleration in SHM depends on angular speed and amplitude.
Hint 2: Insert your amplitude from (d)(i) and $\omega = 1.9\text{ rad s}^{-1}$, checking units give $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use peak SHM acceleration**
In SHM, $a = -\omega^2 x$, so magnitude is largest at maximum displacement: $$ a_0 = \omega^2 x_0 $$

Step 2: **Insert numbers**
$$ a_0 = (1.9)^2 \times 0.23 = 0.83\text{ m s}^{-2} $$ This occurs at the turning points of the shadow.

parts.label: (e)
hints: Hint 1: Think about which way acceleration always points in SHM relative to the equilibrium point P, and what sign of $x$ is needed for acceleration to be in the positive $x$-direction.
parts.proper_answer: Shadow at maximum negative $x$, i.e. point A above left-hand edge of circular path, where acceleration is maximum positive toward P.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find where acceleration is most positive**
Take $x$ positive to the right as in Fig. 1.1. In SHM acceleration is always toward equilibrium: $$ a = -\omega^2 x $$ So positive (rightward) acceleration needs negative (leftward) displacement.

Step 2: **Locate point A**
Maximum positive $a$ is at maximum negative $x$, i.e. $x = -R$. That is the projection of the leftmost point of the circle. Mark A on the screen directly above the left-hand edge of the dashed path, to the left of P.
